evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database)
evidence.text: The database presents Qiu Xigui’s analysis: Shang oracle-bone and bronze forms have a marked blade-like structure, with 一 marking the blade edge; the graph was borrowed for 方 “square.” It reports alternatives: Ye Yusen reads a knife hanging on a rack, Zhu Fangpu sees an early 枋 with a mark on the knife’s holding point, Xu Zhongshu sees a 耒 implement, and He Linyi interprets a line across a blade as dividing with a knife. The page judges some alternatives structurally unconvincing, but the object represented and the proposed derivation from a blade/edge to square remain scholarly analyses, not settled fact.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：方

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database)
evidence.text: The database says oracle-bone and bronze forms are broadly similar. It notes forms with the upper stroke altered to an inverted 工-like shape and sometimes an added short top stroke. It says the small-seal form further changed and the clerical form became the basis for later writing. This account does not establish that every graphic difference is a corruption; the site characterizes the seal form’s development as mistaken transformation.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：方

evidence.source: 《說文解字》 online transcription and 段玉裁 commentary
evidence.text: Xu Shen’s Han-era entry defines 方 as paired boats and explains its form as abbreviated boats with their heads together. Duan Yucai’s Qing commentary distinguishes parallel boats from a raft, then treats raft, comparison, square/round, uprightness, and direction as extensions. These are traditional explanations and a proposed semantic sequence, not direct evidence of the graph’s original form.
evidence.kind: primary historical dictionary transcription with later commentary
evidence.title: 說文解字「方」

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The dictionary reproduces the Shuowen account of paired boats and lists senses including parallel arrangement, comparison, square shape, uprightness, earth, region, direction, method, and temporal adverbial uses. Its citations include the *Shijing* and *Lunyu*. This is evidence that the dictionary tradition records these senses and citations, not a dated chronology of their development.
evidence.title: A01759 方 — 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database)
evidence.text: The database cites Shang oracle-bone records: 合集 28190 uses 方 in a west-direction context; 合集 30394 has 四方 in a ritual context; 合集 36536 and 屯南 2301 use 方 for polities; and 合集 28086 has 方伯 for polity leaders. These are the database’s transcriptions and interpretations of Shang materials. The attestations establish early uses, but they do not by themselves settle whether the uses continue a spatial sense or are phonetic loans.
evidence.kind: secondary scholarly dictionary citing primary inscriptions
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：方

evidence.source: CASE 報科學, National Taiwan University Center for the Advancement of Science Education
evidence.field: Shang spatial readings and graphic proposal
evidence.text: The article discusses 方 in late Shang oracle-bone and bronze material as direction, place or polity, and ritual-related vocabulary. It reports a proposal that the upper stroke marks a blade edge and that the graph was borrowed for square-related meaning, while explicitly calling the graph’s original design unclear. It also discusses later changes in which upper strokes resemble inverted 工 forms. These are interpretations of early inscriptions, not proof that square, direction, and polity senses arose in that order.
evidence.title: 甲骨文的「帝」字與商代的「上帝」（下）

evidence.source: Fudan University Center for Excavated Documents and Paleography
evidence.field: competing glyph analyses and ritual use
evidence.text: The article surveys proposals reading the graph as a knife beside a rack, knife handle, a tool for dividing with a knife, a derivative related to 亡/芒, or a 耒 implement. The author says these readings each have their own reasoning and tentatively suggests a relation to marking boundaries with a sharp implement. It also summarizes disagreements about 方帝: Chen Mengjia reads 方 as a verb for ritual directed to the quarters; Yu Xingwu takes 方帝 as reversed 帝方, with 方 denoting the quarters. This source itself presents the material as unsettled.
evidence.title: 陈广宏‖《汉志》小说与方士关系探原

evidence.field: Western Zhou bronze and Qin manuscript attestations
evidence.text: The database cites Western Zhou bronze evidence for 方 as square in 史逨方鼎, direction in 不𡢁𣪕, land measurement in 召卣, and polity in 人方. It also cites 中山王鼎 for an adverbial use glossed “just/now,” and a Shuihudi Qin strip for 方 as a writing board. The database provides no absolute inscription dates on this page; these are period-labeled artifacts/texts, not a securely dated sequence of semantic change.
evidence.kind: secondary scholarly dictionary citing primary inscriptions and excavated text
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：方

evidence.source: Ministry of Culture, Taiwan, National Cultural Memory Bank
evidence.text: The record describes the Shuihudi Qin slips as excavated in 1975 and written in the late Warring States to early Qin unification period. The cited 方 writing-board example is located by the Chinese Character Database at Shuihudi Qin Law, strip 131; this museum record supplies context for the corpus but does not itself transcribe that strip.
evidence.title: 睡虎地秦簡

evidence.field: borrowed senses and later graph/sense separation
evidence.text: The database describes 方 as borrowed in oracle-bone texts for four directions and polities, and as borrowed for the square sense according to Qiu Xigui’s account. Its claim of a separate original graph □ for square is an etymological analysis. The page does not establish when the borrowing occurred relative to the extant Shang records; nor does it demonstrate a complete semantic pathway from square to region, method, and “just/now.”
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：方

evidence.source: William H. Baxter and Laurent Sagart
evidence.text: The authors’ Old Chinese reconstruction table lists 方 fāng as Middle Chinese pjang, Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *C-paŋ for “square,” and *paŋ for “method” and “just, then.” The table defines MC notation as a convenient representation of information in sources such as the *Guangyun*, not a reconstruction. These are character/reading-specific reconstructions, not direct recordings of Shang pronunciation.
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1

evidence.text: This entry gives 方 as *paŋ in the Zhengzhang system, Yang rhyme group, corresponding to the Guangyun 方 reading. It also notes the proposal that bronze and oracle forms depict an oar/paddle and are an early graph of 榜, while the lower part is a single stroke. That graphic claim differs from the knife and raft analyses and is not independently established by the phonological entry.
evidence.title: 方 — 上古音系

evidence.text: The page reports Zhengzhang-style Old Chinese *baːŋ for 旁 “side” and lists 方 among the same broad phonetic series with *paŋ and *baŋ readings. It also gives modern Mandarin páng and Cantonese Jyutping pòng? [The accessible character entry gives fāng and fong1 for 方; the separate 旁 reading was not independently verified here.] This secondary compilation does not establish that 方 was the original graph for 旁 or that their meanings are cognate. The component 方 in 旁 can plausibly function phonographically given historical sound similarity, but the accessed sources do not establish the detailed chronology or exact sound reading of the compound’s earliest form.
evidence.title: 方 - 维基词典，自由的多语言词典

evidence.source: William H. Baxter and Laurent Sagart
evidence.text: The authors identify the table as Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese version 1.1, dated 20 September 2014, and explain that entries distinguish Mandarin, Middle Chinese transcription, and Old Chinese reconstruction. Their notes caution that the Middle Chinese transcription is not itself a reconstruction and that the Old Chinese forms are reconstructions from comparative evidence.
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1

gaps: The oldest depicted object behind 方 remains disputed: marked blade/edge, a 耒-like implement, paddle/oar, knife-rack or related readings cannot be resolved from the text pages inspected. The object’s original spoken name and pronunciation are not independently recoverable, so no borrowing argument that depends on that name is established.

The proposed derivation from a marked blade/edge to the word 方 “square” is a scholarly hypothesis. No inspected primary inscription demonstrates the object’s name or the sound relationship that would prove this loan.

Shang oracle-bone uses for directions, polities, ritual, and place are reported with corpus numbers, but accessible direct facsimiles and full primary transcriptions were not inspected; the reported uses cannot establish a specific chronology among senses.
The semantic connection among early direction, polity/region, square, method/law, and temporal-adverb senses is not established as a dated chain. Dictionary gloss order was not treated as chronology.

The *Shijing* examples and later received text citations lack securely dated individual manuscript witnesses in the sources inspected; no absolute earliest textual occurrence of each sense was determined.

No component-level etymological account is warranted for 方 as a part of itself; the evidence supports it as a productive sound series in later graphs but this task has no proposed compound component whose independent origin relation can be classified.

The dossier’s pronunciations combine modern Mandarin fāng, Cantonese fong1, Japanese hō/kun readings, Korean pang, Vietnamese phương, and historical data. The external checks here independently confirmed Mandarin and some Chinese historical reconstructions only; they do not establish a single pan-CJK chronology or verify all listed readings.

A proposal that 方 is the original graph of 旁 or that 方 and 旁 are cognate is not verified. Modern/reconstructed sound similarity within a phonetic series does not itself establish graphic ancestry or semantic cognacy.

The isolated dossier claims about dialectal 慌, 仿 variant usage, and English “phon” borrowing were not independently investigated because no reliable source tying those records to a historical formation of 方 was found in the inspected sources.
